articles.title_orig: Nvidia bought itself a little breathing room in the Jensen Huang comeback fight
articles.title_zh: Nvidia bought itself a little breathing room in the Jensen Huang comeback fight
articles.content_orig:
Author of the AI Insider newsletter
Nvidia 's board and interim CEO did just about enough on Tuesday to keep the growing army of Jensen Huang supporters at bay. At least for a few days.
"A clean quarter and guide strengthen the board's hand but do not close the question," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a note to investors after the AI chip giant reported results.
I listened to Nvidia's earnings conference call, and I thought interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones performed well under extraordinary circumstances.
Jones came out swinging. He said the board had no intention of reinstating Huang and made it clear that questions about the ousted CEO were off-limits.
Nvidia shares fell after those comments.
Then Kress quickly delivered some welcome news. Nvidia raised its revenue growth forecast for fiscal 2028. She also pushed back against concerns that the company might have to cut prices to compete, and said profit margins would recover after dipping in the current quarter.
The stock rebounded. By late Tuesday, shares were up almost 5% in after-hours trading.
Jones also said Nvidia would consider internal and external candidates for its next CEO.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
That brings me to the most intriguing moment of the call.
As the question-and-answer session began, Nvidia announced that Ian Buck, VP and president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, would join Kress to answer analysts' questions.
Buck is a serious technologist who helped invent CUDA, the software that makes Nvidia's chips so useful for AI. He's also spent more than two decades at the company and has close relationships with its biggest customers.
Business Insider has a great profile of Buck , who has emerged as a potential successor to Huang.
"His hat is in the ring," Ives said when asked about Buck's appearance on the call.
Now Nvidia appeared to have an almost perfect setup. The board had ruled out Huang's return, Kress had reassured Wall Street about the business, and a respected internal technical leader was being introduced to investors.
Except Buck proceeded to say absolutely nothing.
I kept waiting for an analyst to ask him a question. Nobody did. And Buck never volunteered anything.
If you're being floated as a possible CEO of one of the world's most important companies, and you get a chance to address Wall Street during a leadership crisis, surely you say something?
Maybe Nvidia wants the strong, silent type as its next CEO. (Huang, as we've learned recently, hasn't exactly been the silent type ).
Joking aside, if I were a serious Nvidia investor, I would have wanted to hear from Buck.
"It was odd, but then again this situation is all odd," Ives told me after the call.
Meanwhile, Huang still has powerful, wealthy supporters who aren't going away. And despite the stock gains late Tuesday, Nvidia shares are still below their pre-Huang level — not a great look for the board.
"His return to Nvidia is in all of our best interest," Shopify CEO Tobi Lutke wrote on X after Tuesday's results. He added that there could never be a true replacement for a founder like Huang.
Ives agrees. "The 15% special meeting threshold, activist pressure, and the Commerce Department's position on the export investigation remain the next steps in the saga," he wrote.
Billionaire activist investor Bill Ackman has already explained how shareholders could pressure Nvidia's board to bring Huang back.
Under Nvidia's bylaws, shareholders representing at least 15% of the company's voting power can demand a special shareholder meeting, provided they've held their shares for at least a year.
They could then seek to replace directors with people who support Huang's reinstatement. A new board could then reappoint him CEO.
That's a formidable challenge. Removing directors without cause requires support from two-thirds of Nvidia's outstanding voting shares, according to the company's bylaws .
And 15% of Nvidia, at current valuations, represents more than $500 billion in stock. Huang owns roughly 3.5%, leaving supporters needing another 11.5 percentage points.
Only some of the world's largest investment funds and sovereign wealth funds.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo forgives person who hit him in the eye with rosary in Peru
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo forgives person who hit him in the eye with rosary in Peru
articles.content_orig:
Thankfully, the object did not hit his eye or cause serious harm.
A rosary bracelet thrown from the crowd struck Pope Leo XIV in the face Monday, just below his right eye, as he was traveling in the popemobile through the Las Palmas Air Base in Lima.
The incident occurred following a Mass at the conclusion of his apostolic trip to the country that drew nearly 1.5 million people.
Video footage shows Leo XIV ducking immediately after being hit, clearly reacting to the the impact. Thankfully, the object did not strike his eye or cause serious harm. The pope continued his journey without needing medical assistance.
Following the Mass, Pope Leo headed to the Callao Air Base, from where he departed for Rome, bringing an end to his first pastoral visit to South America as the successor of St. Peter.
Throughout his trip through Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, the Holy Father has shown a remarkable ability to catch — on the fly — rosaries, single-decade rosaries, and other religious devotional items that the faithful often toss toward him.
Although these gestures are typically made with affection and devotion, they also entail risks, especially in large crowds and when the popemobile is moving at higher speeds.
The incident calls attention to the danger that such items being thrown at the pope can pose. What may be an expression of affection for many of the faithful can, in fact, become a risk to the physical safety of the pope and those around him.
This story was first published by EWTN News Español, the Spanish-language sister service of EWTN News. It has been translated and adapted by EWTN News English.

articles.title_orig: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
articles.title_zh: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
articles.content_orig:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams
The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.
On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.
The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.
But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.
Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea , stoking concern about the security of the suneung.
In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.
The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.
Choi has ruled out postponing the exam , which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017 , after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.
Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.
The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.
Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.
To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

articles.title_orig: Beijing: China, Canada agree to 2-year extension of exemptions
articles.title_zh: Beijing: China, Canada agree to 2-year extension of exemptions
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING – China and Canada have agreed to extend relevant exemption measures under a preliminary joint arrangement on bilateral trade issues by two years, China's Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday.
Canada will further expand exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminum products, while China will adjust anti-discrimination measures on certain Canadian agricultural and aquatic products in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, a ministry spokesperson said in response to a media query.
ALSO READ: China expands export control on precursor chemicals to US, Mexico, Canada
Guided by the important consensus reached between the leaders of the two countries, China and Canada have held multiple rounds of economic and trade consultations in the spirit of mutual respect and win-win cooperation, reaching a supplementary joint arrangement on trade issues of mutual concern, the spokesperson said.
The two sides also reached positive consensus on economic and trade issues, including e-commerce cooperation, the establishment of branches of Chinese-funded banks in Canada, and improvements to the business environment, according to the spokesperson.
READ MORE: Commerce ministry: China willing to lengthen cooperation list with Canada
The spokesperson expressed confidence that these arrangements will help deepen bilateral economic and trade cooperation and bring greater benefits to the people of both countries.
Both sides will expedite their respective domestic procedures to put the agreed measures into effect as soon as possible and continue exploring further arrangements to deepen economic and trade cooperation, the spokesperson said.
READ MORE: China and Canada agree to address EV, rapeseed issues
The spokesperson added that the two countries will make full use of the China-Canada Joint Economic and Trade Commission mechanism to expand cooperation, resolve problems, manage differences and promote the sound, stable and sustainable development of bilateral economic and trade relations.
The preliminary joint arrangement between China and Canada was reached during Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to China in January, covering trade issues including electric vehicles, steel and aluminum products, and agricultural and aquatic products.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.content_orig:
The fallout from Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an Nvidia executive that led to his resignation as CEO of Nivida , the company he founded and grew into a $4 trillion chip giant, will likely go on for some time.
But the missteps of Nvidia's board of directors offer immediate lessons, say talent and leadership experts. It shows what happens when there's no clear succession plan, the dangers of an overly decentralized leadership structure, and how companies built around one powerful, controlling leader create the kind of risk boards are responsible for preventing.
In the span of less than a week — from the time Huang admitted that he was unfaithful to his wife until the board announced that he was resigning — the question became: could Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of the AI build-out, operate without him?
With Huang's ouster and the appointment of CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO , Nvidia's employees, customers, and investors will begin to find out. The process will also put a glaring spotlight on why the Nvidia board wasn't better prepared for Huang leaving the company for whatever reason.
"Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical and a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council .
She described what happened at Nvidia as "a failure of epic proportion, both on the part of the board for not fulfilling its fiduciary responsibility to ensure continued viability of the organization by having a robust succession plan, and for the behavior and risks created by the CEO."
"What they're doing now is flying by the seat of their pants," she added.
Nvidia's 10-member board of directors is a collection of early investors, long-time partners and business executives across a range of industries. Before Nov. 12, the company did not have a chair of the board or any clear succession plan . The board also includes directors who expressed "confidence in Jensen" before they had even begun their own independent internal review of his actions.
In addition to naming Kress to the top job, the company appointed Harvey C. Jones, a tech investor and Nvidia director for the past 33 years, as its first-ever chair. After his appointment, the company announced that the board would be conducting a search of both internal and external candidates to find a permanent chief executive.
Alan Fleischmann, founder and CEO of business advisory firm Laurel Strategies and a member of the CNBC CEO Council , says that while "the DNA of any organization is defined by the CEO, there must be a stronger board dynamic and strong leadership surrounding the CEO."
"Succession planning is not simply about identifying who takes over when a CEO leaves," Fleischmann said. "It's about building an institution that can thrive beyond any one individual."
The outsized role Huang played at Nvidia — in September 2025 he told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports — makes it even more difficult for the board to find someone who can understand the inner workings of the company while being such a visible and active hype man for its all-important AI chips.
In corporate governance circles this is known as "key man" risk and it points to a company being overly reliant on one person whose death, departure, or financial or moral compromise could materially damage the organization.
"This is the world's most valuable company and all the risk centered on the shoulders of one man," Calicchio says.
"Flat organizations can be remarkably effective…but there are tradeoffs," Fleischmann added. "When too many decisions, relationships and reporting lines converge around one individual, the organization can become more vulnerable than it appears."
Calicchio acknowledged that a CEO having numerous direct reports isn't problematic in the early days of a company, when the founder knows everyone, but becomes concerning "when a company is the size of Nvidia. I really question the rigor and discipline of their organizational policies."
This same absence of rigor is evident in the lack of any obvious successors to Huang. "You would expect the board to have recognized at some point there was going to be an increasing need to look beyond Jensen," says Tim Wentworth, the former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance and Express Scripts. "This sounds so fundamental, but you don't wait for the rainy day to have the rainy day plan."
Wentworth says that when he was running both Walgreens and Express Scripts, he had a single board member assigned to each one of his direct reports so that "when we had board discussions, somebody in the room could speak about them and their strengths."
At WCG Clinical, succession and talent discussions are done quarterly, says Calicchio. "We're always looking at time frames," she says. "Is this person a definite successor, ready now, or is this someone you're grooming for the long term? Everyone wants to think that replacing the CEO is going to happen in an orderly way, but as we just saw at Nvidia, that's not always the case."
"Boards need to expect the unexpected," she adds.
Huang's powerful grip at Nvidia was great, "until it wasn't," says Wentworth. "It's really hard for a board to have a sense of urgency and the depth of intrusiveness necessary in that process when everything is going great with the company. No one wants to be the contrarian, but that's your job as a board member."

articles.title_orig: Do not eat these breakfast items, says USDA health alert
articles.title_zh: Do not eat these breakfast items, says USDA health alert
articles.content_orig:
Published on Nov. 17, 2026
The issue was discovered when a firm notified FSIS that they had received FDA-regulated item that had been recalled
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is warning consumers not to eat certain ready-to-eat meat products after discovering they may contain an ingredient contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes.
The USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) issued a public health alert on Saturday, Nov. 14, for products containing FDA-regulated biscuits recalled by C.H. Guenther & Son. The issue was discovered after a company notified FSIS that it had received the recalled biscuits. The notice states that the agency may identify additional products as the ingredient recall progresses.
The good news is that no one has reported a confirmed illness linked to the products.
Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images
The affected product is the 9.5-ounce Mmm! Meals Made in Minutes Biscuit & Sausage Gravy. Consumers should check for lot codes or “Use By” dates ranging from Nov. 12 through Nov. 18, 2026, and establishment number EST. 51248. The products were distributed in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Tennessee and Texas. The agency also provided product labels online .
As with most recalls , anyone who purchased the affected products should not eat them. FSIS advises consumers to throw them away or return them to the place of purchase, as is common with recalls . Retailers should also not sell or serve the products.
Listeria can cause listeriosis, a serious infection that, according to the USDA, primarily affects older adults, pregnant women, newborns and people with weakened immune systems. Symptoms can include fever, muscle aches, headache, stiff neck, confusion and loss of balance. In pregnant women, infection can lead to miscarriage, stillbirth, premature delivery or a life-threatening infection in newborns.
People in higher-risk groups who develop flu-like symptoms within two months of eating potentially contaminated food should seek medical care and tell their health care provider about the exposure, the USDA states.
Consumers with questions can contact the USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline at 888-674-6854 or email [email protected] .

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives just as Southeast Asian summit is ending, but still looms over talks
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives just as Southeast Asian summit is ending, but still looms over talks
articles.content_orig:
Trump will participate this week in a trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
See the most recent developments below.
President Donald Trump announced a new trade agreement between the U.S. and the Philippines in Manila on Wednesday, describing it only as a "very big trade deal" without elaborating on the details of the agreement.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for additional information. Trump indicated that the agreement was unexpected.
"We've just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made, by far, And it's a fair deal for both countries, and we're very happy with that," Trump said during the luncheon following a bilateral meeting with Filipino President Ferdinand Marcos.
"And we didn't know that that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly. And it's a magnificent deal for both," Trump said.
-ABC News' Nicholas Kerr, Michelle Stoddart, Fritz Farrow and Meghan Mistry
President Trump arrived at the palace of Philippine President Marcos for a bilateral meeting. Marcos warmly welcomed Trump, but also repeatedly noted how short Trump's visit to the summit is.
"The United States is our only treaty ally, and our relationship has continued to grow and evolve over the many years," Marcos said. "Now we are also exploring new areas of cooperation, particularly in technology, where American leadership and innovation continues to lead the way."
Marcos pointed specifically to artificial intelligence as one of the ways that the Philippines can work more closely with the U.S.
Trump was flanked by some of his top aides, including newly-tapped Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
The president pointed to a few key areas of cooperation, including energy and touted U.S. defense support for the Philippines that the leaders would build on during the visit.
"The United States is now the world's leading producer of oil and natural gas by a lot, and we've just announced a major new pipeline in Alaska to export affordable, abundant supplies of energy to our allies and friends across the Pacific. And the Philippines would be a very natural partner in this effort. We're working on that," Trump said.
Trump, who has long focused on his own renovation projects on the White House, praised the Philippine president's residence.
"We've been there together for a long time. Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes. I love what you've done here. You've done a fantastic job,” Trump said.
President Donald Trump was greeted by Philippine President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Wednesday local time, when the two men met at the historic Malacanang Palace in Manila.
The pair shook hands, exchanged greetings and then walked a short distance before the country’s two national anthems played, alongside a 21-gun salute as the sound of the artillery went off behind them.
Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Trade Rep. Jamieson Greer and Dan Scavino stood nearby on the red carpet throughout the ceremony. The administration officials then shook hands with Marcos.
Cameras captured the two leaders entering the Palace, where President Marcos gave him a brief tour showing him the painting, “The Blood Compact,” which sits prominently at the top of the palace’s Grand Staircase. Marcos also showed several Christmas trees positioned near the painting.
Trump then signed a photo book and turned it around to showcase his message: “This is such a great honor – the U.S.A. loves you!”
President Donald Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a joint trade statement on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, the Philippines, on Tuesday, saying the formal agreement will be finalized "in the coming weeks."
"It's a joint statement agreement between United States of America, the Kingdom of Thailand, on reciprocal trade. It's a very big, actually, it's a very big trade deal," Trump said, after he was asked about the document he signed, given that a formal trade deal has not yet been reached.
"And I look forward to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks," Trump said earlier. "Our staff is working on it very diligently, and it'll be done. But the concept of what we have will be really very permanent, and we're just about there."
The Thai prime minister also pointed out that there is "still more" work to do, but said he is confident an agreement would be reached "soon."
"I believe the agreement will bring greater dynamics to our trade relations and open new opportunities for all stakeholders," Charnvirakul said. "Mr. President, your leadership in bringing this negotiation to a nice conclusion like this is greatly appreciated. Yet there is still a little more to do. I'm confident that the agreement will be ready for us to sign real soon."
According to Trump, Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports under the deal, in addition to removing "substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol, and poultry" and purchasing $2.6 billion in U.S. agricultural products.
Trump said this deal "lays the foundation for much stronger trading relationship that will bring the United States and Thailand closer than ever before," adding that the countries’ current ties are "the closest we’ve ever been."

articles.title_orig: Microsoft aims to challenge OpenAI, Anthropic with cheaper, specialized AI models
articles.title_zh: Microsoft aims to challenge OpenAI, Anthropic with cheaper, specialized AI models
articles.content_orig:
This morning, at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we shared how our vision for Copilot is becoming real for customers. Home , where Chat and Cowork come together, and Office in Copilot are now generally available. Code will become generally available in the coming weeks, while Copilot Managed Runtime for securely hosting and managing apps is now generally available. And Autopilot is beginning to roll out to Frontier customers today. Plus, new plugins and skills built for sales, service, finance, and legal teams are available, as is an expanded Agent 365 platform so you can get even smarter about your intelligence spend.
We’re building Copilot to use raw intelligence to do real work for real people. No single lab is the best at everything, and you shouldn’t have to pick just one. Copilot brings together leading models from across the industry. And with Auto routing, your employees don’t need to worry about picking the right model for every job. Under the hood, Auto dynamically selects the right models and effort for the task, balancing quality, speed, and cost. It saves more power for the moments that need it and spends less when the task doesn’t. Employees can also manually select models from OpenAI or Anthropic, with model access governed by organizational policies.
And Work IQ sets Copilot apart. Knowledge work is fundamentally fragmented and messy. It happens over emails, Teams meetings and chats, Word memos, PowerPoint slide comments, and more. Microsoft 365 holds more than 19.5 exabytes of data, with 90 billion emails, 15 billion Teams messages, and 10 billion new files added every week. Giving a model access to that information isn’t enough. The challenge is identifying and reasoning over what matters for the task at hand. Work IQ solves this problem . It understands what you’re looking for and identifies what you can ignore. The result is accurate, efficient answers that traditional APIs can’t match.
A job is never just one kind of work. You ask questions. You hand things off. You build things. You follow through until they’re done. For years, each of those lived in a different tool. And you were the glue holding it all together. So, we built one place for all of it.
Now generally available, Home is your new starting point in Copilot, where Chat and Cowork come together. As work travels between meetings, chats, documents, emails, apps, and agents, Home keeps you grounded and moving forward. You can review recent activity, get suggestions on what Copilot can help with, and pick up work right where you left off. Ask a quick question in Chat or hand off a whole workflow to Cowork.
Copilot is more powerful without asking you to do more. Home has one composer, powered by Auto , where you can start all your work: tell Copilot what you want to accomplish, and it intelligently routes the work to the right models and effort for the task. For more complex work, Auto may recommend moving from Chat to Cowork. If you agree, Copilot transfers the task seamlessly, helping deliver the outcome with the right level of investment.
Inside Home is a new experience called Today . It’s a command center across mail, calendar, Teams threads, meetings, and tasks. It proactively shows you what you missed, what needs attention now, and what can wait. Today doesn’t just surface the work; it helps you get it done. The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up quickly. Today is currently in private preview in the Copilot app and Outlook.
More and more, AI companies are building their own documents, slides, or spreadsheets. It proves what we’ve known all along: knowledge work runs on Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Copilot has existed in the Office apps for years, and it’s gotten really good. Today, we’re bringing the full power of Office directly into the Copilot app. You can move from idea to a finished document, editing and coauthoring with your teammates. And because every file inherits Microsoft 365 permissions, sensitivity labels, and compliance controls from the start, your work stays protected as you collaborate. This is the only AI tool where you can create a PowerPoint deck or Excel spreadsheet without spinning a meter—all this value is already included in your Copilot subscription license.
We’re expanding what Copilot can do with Autopilot , a trusted autonomous agent that is personal to you, always on, and working for you. Autopilot lives in your tenant and has its own identity, memory, and tools. It shows up where people already work, like Teams, Outlook, chats, channels, and documents, so you can @mention it like a colleague. It can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project—without waiting for a prompt. And it can do things like set up and manage a full supplier review process: building the schedule and workback plan, then handling prep, meetings, and follow-ups on its own, right down to reaching out to stakeholders for updates.
Handing off real work to an agent that acts on its own takes trust. So, Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses. Each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager. IT can scope its access and block it anytime. Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions. You decide what work Autopilot takes on and can check with you before key actions. Autopilot is starting to rollout to customers in Frontier today.
The future of work is people and agent collaboration. Until now, AI interactions have mostly been single player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context. As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work. An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up. Your Autopilot takes a task and checks with you before anything is final. It’s right in the Copilot app, where your files, conversations, people, and agents are all easily accessible. And the collaboration continues in Microsoft Teams. Workspaces is now available in Frontier.
Apps are the new knowledge worker artifact. With Copilot Code , generally available in the coming weeks, the people closest to the problems can now build the solutions. Describe what you want to create in your own words—like an app, an interactive dashboard, or a persistent desktop widget. Copilot picks the best approach and builds it. Share them just as you would a Word document. Apps are securely hosted and managed in your tenant with the Copilot Managed Runtime , generally available today. IT stays in control, with every app visible and managed in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
This is the new Copilot: one place for all the ways you work. And Copilot works even better on Windows , where Hybrid Intelligence allows Copilot to ground itself in all the context on your local PC, complete local actions, and even offload the right work to models running locally on your PC, saving you time and money.
But none of it matters until Copilot creates real value inside your business. Today nearly 80% of the Fortune 500 companies use Cowork.
At medicine company Lilly, the team is using Copilot for multi-step research and analysis to shorten the path to real breakthroughs. The team has spent decades pushing science to make conditions that are incurable today, treatable tomorrow. More than 5,000 people at Lilly are using Copilot Cowork every month, including the team of scientists, who now hand Cowork multistep research tasks that identify the most promising paths before the lab work begins. articles.title_orig: Cyber agency warns of ‘critical’ vulnerability in Java programming language
articles.title_zh: Cyber agency warns of ‘critical’ vulnerability in Java programming language
articles.content_orig:
Oracle is preparing to release security patches for 11 vulnerabilities in Java SE on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, all of which may be exploited remotely without authentication, as separate reports warn of a potentially critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw affecting OpenJDK.
The 11 vulnerabilities carry a maximum CVSS 3.1 severity score of 8.1, according to Oracle's advance security notice . The company has not disclosed their CVE identifiers, affected components, or the individual consequences of exploitation.
The separate OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 , has reportedly been assigned a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later. However, those details remain unconfirmed, and there is no evidence yet that the reported flaw is among the 11 vulnerabilities Oracle plans to patch.
Security firm Calif said in a post on X that it discovered and reported the flaw, which it calls Java4Shell , and that the vulnerability had leaked. Calif said it would publish technical details by 1 p.m. Pacific time on November 17, after Oracle releases a patch.
Security company watchTowr acknowledged the reports in a post on X , but cautioned that the technical details were still unconfirmed.
Separate analyses of the OpenJDK source code by security companies Upwind and Equixly point to a flaw in Java's Base64 decoder whose likely result is a crash of the Java virtual machine (JVM) rather than code execution.
The vulnerability's CVE record remains reserved without a public description. No official advisory has specified the vulnerable component, precise exploitation requirements, affected version range, or the availability of a fix.
Oracle's ops.java site now lists the replacement builds below as its current releases. Oracle's advance notice, release notes and download page still showed the earlier builds as of 16:59 UTC.
Oracle advises customers to stop using its current builds of Java 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, and 27 after the November 17 security update and move to the corresponding replacement releases.
The company's Java release notes contain the update guidance, while ops.java lists the following planned builds:
The November security notice identifies the following affected Oracle products and versions:
Oracle says all 11 Java SE vulnerabilities may be exploited over a network without requiring credentials. That does not necessarily mean they all allow remote code execution or that every application running an affected Java version can be attacked directly.
The advance notice does not identify the vulnerable Java components or specify what an attacker could accomplish by exploiting each flaw.
Oracle also warns that the information may change before the complete security advisory is published.
The reported CVE-2026-114938 vulnerability introduces a separate concern for organizations operating Java applications, particularly those exposed to the internet.
However, the public information does not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed.
However, Oracle's notice and the OpenJDK advisories do not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed.
Upwind said in a technical analysis that its reading of the OpenJDK source points to a flaw in Java's AVX-512 Base64 decoder, and Equixly reached the same finding in a separate analysis . The flawed code runs only on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support, when untrusted data reaches the basic or URL decoder of java.util.Base64 . ARM servers do not run it.
The code is in Java 17.0.6 and later and in Java 21, 25 and 27, but not in standard Java 8 or 11. A crash is the likely result because the bytes written past the buffer are fixed and not chosen by the attacker. Neither firm reported reproducing the overflow on AVX-512 hardware.
Oracle's 8u371-perf release notes show that its Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack added a "Base64 Decoding optimization for x86 using AVX-512". Neither firm said whether the Performance Pack is affected.
Both firms named two JVM options as stopgaps to keep the flawed code from running: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics , which turns off the Base64 intrinsics, and -XX:UseAVX=2 , which turns off all AVX-512 code paths and can slow other work. Neither option has been confirmed by a vendor for this flaw, the firms said.
Oracle's November notice covers Oracle products and does not establish the patch status of third-party OpenJDK distributions.
The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group , which coordinates security disclosures affecting OpenJDK source code, had not published an advisory newer than October 24 at the time of the earlier review.
Until official details are available, organizations cannot determine from the reported CVE alone whether their Java deployments are vulnerable or which specific update addresses the issue.
Oracle began a monthly security patch cycle on May 28, introducing targeted security releases between its quarterly Critical Patch Updates.
Its Java security update plan , last updated September 10, identified November 17 as the next scheduled monthly release.
Organizations should inventory deployed Java runtimes, identify internet-facing applications, and prepare to test and install the relevant vendor updates once they become available.
This is a developing story. We will update this article as Oracle publishes its full vulnerability advisory and additional verified details about CVE-2026-114938, affected versions, and available patches emerge.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia earnings live: Nvidia posts Q3 beat as revenue rose 103% YOY to $115.8B, board says it will not reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia earnings live: Nvidia posts Q3 beat as revenue rose 103% YOY to $115.8B, board says it will not reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia .
The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang , became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier.
Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August.
By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear.
Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight.
Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18 , the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported .
Trump on Monday denied being briefed . Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.
The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz . Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone , compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis.
A White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump's portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to "avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest." The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence.
Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war .
"Look, we have the highest stock market we've ever had," Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans' midterm losses .
Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500's 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year's performance.
Huang's rise in Trump's Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia's on Wall Street. The two have met or appeared together at least 15 times since Trump returned to office, according to a CNBC review of public records and news reports. Huang in June told The Associated Press that Trump even "calls me in the middle of the night."
It wasn't always that way.
At Trump's Jan. 20, 2025, inauguration, several Silicon Valley titans occupied prime seats, but Huang wasn't there. The two men had never met.
That changed on Jan. 31, 2025, when Huang visited the White House, capping a bruising week for Nvidia: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek had wiped $593 billion off the company's market value in a single day, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters .
Two days before the meeting, Trump's money managers bought between $1 million and $5 million in Nvidia stock .
For Huang, much of the relationship hinged on access to China. In April 2025, the administration effectively halted sales of Nvidia's H20 chips to China, prompting a $4.5 billion charge , according to an SEC filing. Huang argued that withholding U.S. chips would only accelerate China's development of its own.
The administration eventually relented. After another meeting with Trump in July 2025, Huang announced from Beijing that Nvidia expected to resume H20 sales . A week after Trump confirmed an August 2025 deal calling for 15% of the revenue from the company's chip sales to China to go to the U.S. government, his accounts also bought between $5 million and $25 million in Nvidia stock, one of several large tech investments that day.
Huang was also becoming a fixture of Trump's international diplomacy, joining him in Saudi Arabia and the U.K. Nvidia, already a $1 million donor to Trump's inaugural fund , would pledge another $25 million to his planned White House ballroom on condition of anonymity, The Washington Post first reported .
But behind the scenes, intelligence officials first briefed Trump last fall on Huang's relationship with the woman suspected of spying for China, The New York Times reported .
Trump nevertheless continued to ease restrictions on Nvidia's business in China, announcing Dec. 8 that the company could sell its more powerful H200 chips . His accounts had sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock four days earlier and bought more the day after.
In the first eight months of 2026, Trump's accounts made another 38 Nvidia trades worth a combined $9.4 million to $28.3 million, according to CNBC's analysis. A disclosure released Oct. 8 — the day Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science — showed purchases of up to $1.6 million and sales of up to $1 million in August alone.
Trump stood by Huang as Nvidia's board weighed his future last week, urging him to fight to keep his job , the Times reported.
With Huang out and Nvidia's shares tumbling, Trump described him Thursday as a "tremendous talent" who was "going through hell" — in the same interview in which he boasted of the market's record highs.
Trump is already floating a comeback for Huang, telling reporters Monday that reinstating him "certainly isn't a bad idea." But Nvidia's board is not considering his return , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because they were discussing internal matters."

articles.title_orig: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.title_zh: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett .
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden .
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

articles.title_orig: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages
articles.title_zh: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages
articles.content_orig:
Chief Correspondent covering media and technology
Did AI cause the US government to shut down all air travel Friday?
Could be, says the US government.
Also, maybe not. Who knows? But don't worry.
That's the confusing answer from Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. He went on Fox News on Monday and said that the nationwide grounding last week — as well as other recent high-profile outages at places like JPMorgan, Microsoft , and United — might have all stemmed from organizations introducing new AI software into their IT stacks.
Why does he think that? Because "one guy that's very smart with tech," — not Elon Musk, Mullin specified — told him that. And "that kinda makes sense to me."
I mean, it also kinda makes sense to me? Maybe? But I'm not running a federal agency with more than 200,000 workers and an annual budget of more than $100 billion.
But Mullin said he really doesn't know. He does know that "we just have a lot of technologists [sic] thrown at us and our world runs on technology now. We used to have backup systems. And the backup systems are overwhelmed by the new systems now."
Then Mullin told Fox viewers that they should "breathe." And be assured that the US is probably not under a cyber attack — something he felt "98%" confident about.
I would very much like to live in a world where a top federal official doesn't muddle through national news interviews about outages. I would very much like to live in a world where the administration hadn't spent much of last year telling us the federal government was incompetent and should be radically downsized . Because sometimes we really want the federal government — not "one guy" — to be able to tell us what's actually happening inside these complicated systems, and what should be done about it.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
But I also think we'd have these exact same problems if we had the most competent, well-meaning public servants in charge right now.
That's because all of this stuff is gnarly and complicated. Long before the AI boom, we've had technologists pointing out how rickety and poorly maintained much of America's digital and physical infrastructure is — and how seemingly isolated problems can have enormous ripple effects. Perhaps you recall the giant blackout of 2003 , where big swaths of the country, including New York City, lost power because of a software glitch in Ohio.
Now we've added AI to the mix —a technology so new and head-scratching that the people who are building it frequently say they're not really sure how it works , and aren't exactly sure how to control it .
Which is why people who have talked to more than "one guy" often tell us to buckle up for more instability. "We should plan to wake up in Software Beirut, where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time," as journalist Josh Tyrangiel put it in The Atlantic .
What can you, a normal person, do about this? Here I agree with Markwayne Mullin: You shouldn't do anything. There's nothing much you can do, aside from the digital equivalent of making sure you have some soup cans and water bottles handy, just in case.
But if you're a member of the media — that is, anyone with access to a keyboard and an internet connection — things get a little trickier. It is reasonable to cover all of these outages, ask why they're happening, and not accept the hand-wavy answers you often get right after an event. But also be ready to accept that sometimes things break because things break, and that sometimes a coincidence is a coincidence. Or that maybe it's all a squirrel's fault .
That's not an easy balance to pull off. Ring the bell every time there's a possible threat, and you'll end up with a country that's permanently on edge — or worse, doesn't pay attention to any warnings at all. Wait too long before ringing the bell, and people may be woefully unprepared. It's a real challenge .
That said, one very easy step is to just stay mute when you don't have anything helpful to say.
Tuesday morning, I got asked to come on an interview show to discuss "the November 17 blackout," which confused me since I was unaware there had been a blackout Tuesday.
Turns out it was a reference to a made-up thing on social media , and I'm not going to spend more time discussing a non-thing here.
Except to say that it's one thing for your uncle to pass along a hoax email to his friends and family. And it's another to go on TV or the internet and give the hoax that much more oxygen. Even if you're ostensibly going to debunk the hoax, you're still spreading the particulates around.
But Markwayne Mullin? I'd definitely like you to ask a few more people — perhaps there are still technology experts in your organization, for starters — for more information. Then come back and tell us what you've learned. We'd love to know more.

articles.title_orig: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
articles.title_zh: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
articles.content_orig:
"Opening the door to uncontrolled immigration," is how Reform UK described it. "Dragging us into the European Union via the back door," was the charge levelled by the Conservatives.
You could be forgiven for expecting drastic change come Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels judging by some of the criticism levelled by opponents of the Labour government.
Instead, what's on the table is a limited youth work and mobility scheme (the source of Reform's ire), agreement on cross-channel carbon emissions pricing and a deal to ease food trade.
There's also talk of reducing tuition fees for EU students at British universities (something EU member states, like Germany, really want) in exchange for the UK being admitted to an EU manufacturing scheme (which is important to the Burnham government).
Even in these limited areas, I'm told, not all details will be ironed out by the time of Thursday's meeting.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted last week this is all a "step" towards a closer working relationship with Europe.
It's certainly not a leap, and definitely not a matter of rejoining the bloc at this stage.
Other "steps" under immediate discussion are the UK rejoining the EU's electricity market, and the UK trying again to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme.
"Small steps… to make both sides stronger," is how the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas describes this process. She also warns: "We have in Europe a lot of trauma from Britain leaving [the EU], so things will not be easy."
Bigger, potentially more politically explosive EU-UK questions look likely to follow after Friday's summit. It's thought Burnham may propose rejoining the EU's customs union and/or the single market. There are suggestions he could eventually table a new referendum on rejoining the EU. None of this before the next general election, though.
On this side of the Channel, the debate is very much focused on what Britain might want. Burnham's plan is bold, belated or completely barmy - depending on your political perspective. But there's been little discussion about the EU point of view, and less still on how the EU has changed since Britain left it.
Just how different is the EU in 2026 from the bloc Britain turned its back on a decade ago? And with the UK still mired in arguments over its relationship with Europe, does the EU even want GB back in the fold or would Brussels now rather avoid more drama?
Since 2016, a series of international shocks have fundamentally changed the EU.
The Covid crisis collapsed international supply chains. Europe became aware just how dependent it was on China for medical supplies, for example. Then, Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine showed the EU how utterly reliant many members were on energy supplies from Moscow. Big EU beasts like Germany and Italy were particularly affected.
The Ukraine war, the continent's biggest active conflict since World War Two, has persuaded the EU that Europe's domestic defence industry and industrial policy needs a boost and far better coordination.
Donald Trump's two stints as US president convinced the EU that it can never again fully rely on the US to be Europe's best friend abroad, either in trade or security terms. And China's attempt to 'dump' cheap cars and steel in Europe, hurting the Continent's businesses, has made the EU more protectionist-minded.
Brussels's main takeaways: Europe should become more self-reliant. And where imports are needed - with fossil fuels, for example - it must diversify which countries it buys from.
The French used to be a lone voice amongst big EU countries, pushing for more protectionism. Other member states prioritised finding the lowest possible prices, as was once the case with Russian gas, for example. Now there's a growing acceptance that economic efficiency must at times be sacrificed to achieve security of supply.
Some think the UK won't want to align itself with an increasingly protectionist, borrow-happy bloc. While an EU member, the free-trade-minded UK was credited with pushing Brussels to be more "British" and make its single market more competitive.
Others point out that Britain has also changed since 2016.
"The British are less 'British' than they once were," Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform, told me. When the EU introduced steel tariffs to protect itself against Chinese dumping, the UK followed suit with its own, similar tariffs. Now, the EU is placing high tariffs on Chinese imports of electric vehicles - and once again the UK is considering a similar move. "Everyone is a bit more French now," says Grant.
Another big EU change, according to European policy expert Georgina Wright, is that EU citizens have become more comfortable with the idea of centralised European power: a pooling of sovereignty in times of emergency.
The Covid crisis prompted the EU to embrace 'common borrowing', where Brussels raises debt on behalf of member states, who then share the benefits and the risks. It was a historic move, particularly for Germany which was once allergic to the idea. Now there's discussion about a new round of common borrowing focused on defence, in answer to Russian aggression and a US proposing to withdraw defence capabilities from Europe.
Some in the EU tell me that none of this would be possible had the more sovereign-minded UK remained a member state.
But there are political winds of change blowing through the bloc.
Nationalist, more Eurosceptic parties are polling strongly in big EU members states ahead of upcoming elections. The EU that Burnham wants Britain to align with might look very different by the end of next year.
In France, one of the EU's two most influential countries, the hard-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls ahead of the spring presidential election. Nation-first parties in Italy, Spain and Poland, as in France, say they want to transform the bloc from the inside.
Britain's centre-left government - as well as some UK voters - might be put off by an EU with Le Pen as a dominant force.
Conversely, there's an argument that an EU led by Eurosceptics might actually become more appealing to Britain. While those parties have their differences, they generally want to take powers back from Brussels, making the EU a looser club of stronger nation states - less of a political project, and more of a transactional club of common economic interests.
One change we can pretty much bet on is this: if Le Pen becomes French president, Brussels will become embroiled in internal existential tussles over the EU's future. These fault lines will pit the left against the right; pro-Europeans against Eurosceptics; Ukraine backers against those (like Le Pen) who want to stop financial aid; fans of a bigger EU budget against parties wanting to slash national contributions.
With all that going on, negotiations with the UK would very likely slip further down the priority list. British diplomats might find their calls unanswered.
If Burnham really wants to get closer to the EU, the time to act is now, says Wright. She identifies a window of opportunity before France's election for the UK to get "creative" in its re-set proposals.
Brussels is certainly under pressure to be more flexible in its relations with trusted allies outside the bloc, because of the threatening geopolitical climate. The EU embrace of Canada is a clear example.
"The prime minister should get out and about on the continent more, be more visible and talk more positively about what can be done together," says Wright.
Wright insists people in the UK are open to the idea. She quotes a survey by the National Centre for Social Research, published this month, which suggests 42% of Britons prioritise closer links with Europe over the US, while only 9% of Britons prioritise links with the US.
Then there's the question of how much Brussels actually wants Britain back in the European bloc.
Some in the UK believe they could take advantage of current geopolitical uncertainty. W

articles.title_orig: Jeff Bezos has tips for the Nvidia board in choosing a successor for Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Jeff Bezos has tips for the Nvidia board in choosing a successor for Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
A pivotal Nvidia earnings call offered a crucial clue as to who could succeed Jensen Huang .
After prepared remarks from interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones during Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday, a notable participant was introduced: Ian Buck , Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, who joined Kress for the Q&A session.
Buck, an Nvidia veteran who helped invent its CUDA software for AI chips, had been floated by industry observers as a potential successor to Huang . He didn't end up saying anything on the call.
His appearance came as Jones reiterated that Nvidia's board does not intend to reinstate Huang and that the board hired the search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find his successor from both internal and external candidates.
"We want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person," Jones said.
Buck has worked at Nvidia for more than two decades. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan previously told Business Insider that Buck was one of Huang's three "right-hand men" — along with Kress and senior VP of GPU engineering Jonah Alben.
That said, Stephen Witt, who wrote a biography on Huang, said Buck is less focused on business strategy.
"He's more like the world's best mechanic," Witt said.
Earlier in the day, Huang broke his silence and expressed his desire to return to the company — so long as the board approved.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
On the call, Jones said the company would not take questions on the circumstances of Huang's resignation or the ongoing investigation. That said, Kress addressed it briefly when talking about the impacts on employee retention.
She said there are "diverse opinions," though employees remain committed to their work.
Huang's ouster has sent shockwaves through the AI sector, the broader markets, and the global economy. The stock has plunged as investors try to get to grips with a future without the vision, connections, and technical knowledge of Huang, who led the company for more than 30 years.
Melius Research analyst Ben Reitzes called Buck Nvidia's strongest potential internal successor given his work on CUDA, stewardship of the chip giant's massive data center business, and relationships with top cloud customers.
Business Insider asked Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., whether putting Buck on the earnings call signaled that this Nvidia executive is a candidate for the new CEO role.
"His hat is in the ring," Ives said.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft calls Copilot "the new OS for work" at Ignite keynote
articles.title_zh: Microsoft calls Copilot "the new OS for work" at Ignite keynote
articles.content_orig:
Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”
The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.
The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside them.
Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability.
Also announced as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ , an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ , a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.
Copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment currently available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella said that “Until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”
Trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s new frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he said.
In a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft says each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.
The promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and users to place their trust in the company’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure will still have to be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will have to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.
Along with the guardrails, Microsoft announced what it calls the “ AI Transparency Initiative .” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and Mastercard, to develop open, industrywide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”
Along with the other announced additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365 , its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The new agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft says is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”
Along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics : “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” said Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend, and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model , and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less .”
Nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for users across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he said. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”
That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “ community-first AI infrastructure plan .” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.
